Q: Why does __USE_MISC and M_PI get undefined by stdio.h and math.h respectively? A:

How do I get M_PI to be defined, if __USE_MISC is not supposed to be specified by the user?

A key thing to understand here is that M_PI is not specified by any version of the C language, and it is of a form that is not reserved. This means that, absent some extension or additional specification on top of C itself, a C program can expect to use that identifier for its own purposes -- variable name, function name, structure member name, etc. For example, perhaps it declares const unsigned int M_PI = 0x03A0;, which would break if M_PI were defined as a macro expanding to a floating point constant. It is the objective of GCC's strict conformance modes, such as -std=c23 or -ansi, that GCC will accept every program that conforms strictly to the specified version of the language, which is inconsistent with providing M_PI as a pre-defined macro.

On the other hand, M_PI has traditionally been defined in math.h by C implementations for UNIX-like systems, and it is specified by POSIX. GCC and Glibc were designed first and foremost to target GNU's UNIX-like environment, so by default, they do provide an M_PI definition in math.h. -std=c23 turns this off, so one alternative is simply to omit that.

Another alternative is to use one of GCC's extended modes instead of a strict conformance mode. For example, -std=gnu23. GCC's default is one of these (which one it is in particular varies with the version of GCC).

Yet another alternative is to define an appropriate feature test macro in source files that need it. __USE_MISC is not appropriate for this, as it is reserved for implementation use, and neither GCC nor Glibc documents any use for it in source files. Glibc does, however, document several feature-test macros that would be appropriate, and some of these will be relevant to other C implementations, too. Each of these feature-test macro definitions does the trick for me with GCC 15.2.1 and Glibc 2.42, in combination with gcc -std=c23 (you can choose any one or more):

#define _XOPEN_SOURCE
#define _GNU_SOURCE
#define _DEFAULT_SOURCE

The feature test macro(s) should be defined at the very top of the source file, before any #include directives. Each of these will cause a definition of M_PI to be exposed by math.h, but they differ in which other library extensions they enable.

Or you can just define your own, which is the most portable option available. For example,

#ifndef M_PI
#define M_PI 3.14159265358979323846
#endif

Q: Genetic algorithm for kubernetes allocation A:

This is a straightforward bin packing problem. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bin_packing_problem Why tackle it with a genetic algorithm!?! That is going to be horribly slow, especially if you use python.

Implementing a standard bin packing algorithm in a native language with a decent optimizing compiler will give performance many orders of magnitude faster - a millisecond or two for your sample problem

Here is the C++ code for the implementation of the first-fit decreasing bin packing algorithm with dual resources

void packBestFirstFit()
{
    // sort items in order of decreasing largest resource requirement sum

    std::sort(
        theItems.begin(), theItems.end());
    std::reverse(
        theBins.begin(), theBins.end());

    // sort bins in order of increasing capacity sum

    std::sort(
        theBins.begin(), theBins.end());

    // fit each item into the smallest bin that fits

    for (cThing &item : theItems)
    {
        for (cThing &bin : theBins)
        {
            if (item.myRes1 > bin.myRes1 ||
                item.myRes2 > bin.myRes2)
                continue;

            bin.pack(item);

            break;
        }
    }
}

Q: Animatore issue after upgrading project A:

It basically means that your code is trying to start an animation on a view that is not attached to the window.

Every view in Android has a window token, which is only available when the view is attached to a window. So maybe animating view in onCreate() before the view is laid out, or animating view inside fragment before onviewCreate() or after onDestroyView().

Please explain your code structure in more details if possible.

Regard, V

Q: change default environment from (base) to (env) in conda/anaconda in Ubuntu A:

There is now (2026) a way to change the default environment activated by conda, including the one activated by the init code in .bashrc.

First create your default environment. I've called my preferred enviroment default on my systems.

Then set the default_activation_env conda configuration option:

conda config --set default_activation_env default

Next time you source .bashrc, e.g. when creating a terminal, the default environment will be activated.

(I use the c-forge miniconda, but I believe this should work on Anaconda as well).

Q: Unable to Load google/gemma-3-27b-it on 3 x RTX 3090 GPUs using TGI in Docker A:

The issue is likely related to how NCCL allocates memory for inter-GPU communication buffers on top of the model weights.

Gemma-3-27B memory requirements:

  • Full precision (FP32): ~108 GB — won't fit on 3x 24GB

  • Half precision (FP16/BF16): ~54 GB — fits on 3x 24GB in theory, but NCCL + KV cache + activation memory push it over

  • The .safetensors files being 44GB suggests the weights are already in FP16/BF16

Why it fails with 72GB total across 3 GPUs:

Even though 54GB < 72GB, TGI + NCCL need additional memory for:

  • NCCL communication buffers (~1-2GB per GPU)

  • KV cache for inference

  • CUDA context (~500MB per GPU)

  • Activation memory during forward pass

This leaves very little headroom on 24GB cards when splitting a 27B model.

Solutions:

  1. Use --dtype float16 or --dtype bfloat16 explicitly to ensure FP16 loading:

     --dtype float16 --num-shard 3

  2. Set --max-batch-prefill-tokens and --max-total-tokens lower to reduce KV cache allocation:

     --max-total-tokens 2048 --max-batch-prefill-tokens 2048

  3. Use quantization — with 3x 24GB GPUs, 4-bit quantization (AWQ/GPTQ) would comfortably fit the model on a single GPU:

     --quantize awq --num-shard 1

  4. Check RTX 3090 peer-to-peer support — NCCL sharding works best with NVLink. RTX 3090s communicate over PCIe, which can cause issues. Set:

     -e NCCL_P2P_DISABLE=1

For reference, the RTX 3090 has 24GB GDDR6X with 936 GB/s bandwidth — you can check full specs and compare with other GPUs at gpuark.com.

Disclosure: I contribute to gpuark.com.

Q: Why does Apache PDFBox use SHA-1? Is it still secure? A:

I don't know what you mean by "LTV Process"

I'd assume the OP here means they add validation related information to the PDF so that the next validator can use that information instead of having to retrieve it online. Example profiles for this are PAdES-LT and PAdES-LTA by ETSI, PAdES-A by ISO, and LTV-enabled by Adobe. The aim is allowing for Long Term Validation of the signature even after the original PKI has shut down.

In the context of PDFBox the AddValidationInformation class is used for this.

but it is not relevant where you found / or found out about SHA-1.

Yes, it is! Use of SHA-1 for the VRI keys in the PDF DSS is not a security issue while use in signatures themselves meanwhile is.
